title: Versioned Structs and Function Tables
summary: Sometimes callers need to see a struct, such as an options block. Windows' trick is to start every such struct with its own **size**, so the library can tell which version the caller was built with. The same idea, applied to a struct full of function pointers, gives a **function table** that can grow across versions.
markdown:
## The problem with visible structs

A creation function with many options is clumsy with a long parameter list. A struct is nicer:

```cpp-norun
typedef struct xenon_world_options
{
    int32_t width;
    int32_t height;
    int32_t gravity;
} xenon_world_options;

XENON_API int32_t xenon_world_create_ex(const xenon_world_options* options, xenon_world** out);
```

Then version 2 needs a `seed`. Add it to the struct, and a program compiled against version 1 passes a 12-byte struct where version 2 reads 16. The `seed` comes from whatever memory follows: garbage.

## Size first

The Win32 API's answer, used by hundreds of its structs (`cbSize` in `WNDCLASSEXW`, `dwSize` in many others): the **first member is the size of the struct, filled in by the caller**.

```cpp-norun
typedef struct xenon_world_options
{
    uint32_t size;      // the caller sets this to sizeof(xenon_world_options)
    int32_t  width;     // version 1
    int32_t  height;    // version 1
    int32_t  gravity;   // version 1
    uint32_t seed;      // version 2: added at the END
} xenon_world_options;
```

The caller always writes:

```cpp-norun
xenon_world_options options{};
options.size = sizeof(options);
options.width = 64;
```

A program compiled against version 1 sets `size` to 16; one compiled against version 2 sets 20. The library reads only the fields that fit:

```cpp-norun
int32_t xenon_world_create_ex(const xenon_world_options* options, xenon_world** out)
{
    if (!options || options->size < offsetof(xenon_world_options, seed)) return fail(XENON_INVALID_ARGUMENT, "options too small");
    WorldSettings s;
    s.width   = options->width;
    s.height  = options->height;
    s.gravity = options->gravity;
    // a field is present if the struct reaches past its end
    s.seed = options->size >= offsetof(xenon_world_options, seed) + sizeof(options->seed) ? options->seed : 12345u;
    ...
}
```

`offsetof(T, member)` is the byte position of a member, from `<stddef.h>`. A member is present when `size >= offsetof(T, member) + sizeof(member)`.

The rules that make this work:

- New members only ever go **at the end**.
- Never remove, reorder or resize a member.
- Every new member has a **sensible default** for callers who did not send it.
- A size **bigger** than the library knows (a newer program with an older DLL) is fine: read what you know, ignore the rest. Or reject it if you cannot honour fields you do not understand; decide and document.

## Function tables

The same trick works for a whole interface. Instead of exporting thirty functions, export **one** that returns a table of function pointers:

```cpp-norun
typedef struct xenon_api
{
    uint32_t size;                                              // of this table
    uint32_t version;                                           // e.g. 2
    int32_t (*world_create)(xenon_world** out);
    void    (*world_destroy)(xenon_world* world);
    int32_t (*world_add_stone)(xenon_world*, int32_t, int32_t, int32_t);
    // version 2:
    int32_t (*world_save)(const xenon_world*, const char* path);
} xenon_api;

XENON_API const xenon_api* xenon_get_api(uint32_t wantedVersion);
```

A program asks for the version it was built for. The library returns its table if it is at least that new, or `NULL` if it is too old. The program checks `size` before touching later members. This is how Vulkan, OpenXR and many game engines expose their APIs, and it suits plugins (milestone 5): one `GetProcAddress` gets everything.

## Common mistakes

> [!warning] Forgetting to set size
> A zero size makes the library reject or misread the struct. Many APIs return an error for that; yours should too.

> [!warning] Inserting a new member in the middle
> Every member after it moves, so old programs' values land in the wrong fields. Always append.

## Check yourself
```quiz
? What are the rules for growing a versioned struct?
- Add members wherever they fit best, as long as `size` is updated
+ Add members only at the end, never remove, reorder or resize one, and give each new member a default
- Add members at the start so old members keep their meaning, and bump `size`
- Replace members that are no longer needed with new ones of the same size
> Old programs know the old offsets, so every existing member must stay where it is, and callers that did not send a new member need a sensible default.

? How does the library decide whether a member is present in the caller's struct?
- It checks that the member's value is nonzero
- It compares the caller's `size` with `sizeof` of the newest struct it knows
+ It checks that the caller's `size` is at least the member's offset plus the member's size
> `size >= offsetof(T, member) + sizeof(member)`. A nonzero value says nothing, and comparing with the whole newest struct would reject every older caller.

? Why are function tables popular for plugin and graphics APIs?
+ One exported function gives the whole interface, and the table itself can be versioned and grown
- Calls through a function pointer are faster than calls through the import table
- Function pointers do not need a calling convention
> One `GetProcAddress` gets everything, and the table starts with `size` and `version` like any versioned struct.

? Why does a versioned struct start with its size?
- To make the struct line up on an 8-byte boundary
- Because C requires the size to be the first member of a struct
+ So the library can tell which members the caller's version of the struct contains
> Old callers send smaller sizes, and the library only reads what is there.

? A member `seed` sits at offset 16 and is 4 bytes. The caller's size is 16. Is `seed` present?
- Yes, because the size reaches offset 16
+ No, it would need a size of at least 20
- Only if `seed` is nonzero
> Present means size >= offset + sizeof(member), so 16 + 4 = 20 bytes at least.

? What does a function table export instead of many separate functions?
- One DLL per function, loaded on demand
- A `.def` file that lists every function's address
+ One function returning a versioned struct of function pointers
> The table can grow like any versioned struct, and the caller asks for the version it was built for.
```
ideas:
- Add `xenon_world_options` with a `size` member to your library. Build a "version 1" program, then add `seed` and check the old program still gets the default.
- Expose your library through `xenon_get_api` and write a program that loads the DLL with one `GetProcAddress` call.
